desc:
A long corridor has n seats and n students, all standing on integer positions of a number line. seats[i] is the position of the i-th seat and students[j] is the starting position of the j-th student. Several seats, or several students, may share a position.

Every student must end up on a different seat. In one move a single student walks one unit to the left or to the right (students may pass through each other and stand on the same spot while moving). Return the minimum total number of moves needed to seat everybody.

seats = [3, 1, 5], students = [2, 7, 4]       -> 4
seats = [4, 1, 5, 9], students = [1, 3, 2, 6] -> 7
seats = [2, 2, 6, 6], students = [1, 2, 3, 6] -> 4

In the first example, seats at 1, 3, 5 are matched with students at 2, 4, 7, which costs 1 + 1 + 2.
hints: Any assignment of students to seats is allowed, and the cost of a pairing is the distance between the two positions. Which pairing minimizes the total distance?
If a student A stands left of a student B but is sent to a seat that is right of B's seat, the two walks cross. What happens to the total if you uncross them?
Sort both arrays and match them index by index: the leftmost student takes the leftmost seat, and so on. The answer is the sum of |seats[i] - students[i]| after sorting.
editorial: Sort the seats and the students. Then the student with the i-th smallest position takes the seat with the i-th smallest position, and the answer is the sum of the absolute differences.

Why: take two students a ≤ b and two seats x ≤ y. Matching them as (a,y) and (b,x) (crossed) never costs less than matching (a,x) and (b,y), because on a line the crossed pairing walks the overlapping stretch twice. Repeatedly uncrossing any crossed pair never increases the cost and ends with the sorted matching, so that matching is optimal.
Sorting costs O(n log n), the final sum is O(n).
